extracted.intended_audience: architects, artists, art critics, and students of art/architecture (especially those interested in Gothic theory and Victorian art criticism)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Ruskin's evaluative principles for architecture and visual art—principles about variety vs monotony, naturalism vs design, originality, function, and moral temperament in representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper form / observance of legal forms
rubrics_metrics.description: One form of the said capitals is proper, and no other; ... take care that the legal forms are observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical commissions sometimes demand adherence to an accepted 'proper form' (e.g., capitals of the proper form and quantity). This is acceptable for ensuring correctness and convenience of housing, but it is a limited, manufacture-like approach and may not by itself produce great art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture should be correct and entertaining
rubrics_metrics.description: We may require of an architect, as we do of a novelist, that he should be not only correct, but entertaining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond technical correctness and propriety, architecture should engage and delight the observer; aesthetic interest and novelty are legitimate expectations of an architect's work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality — art must 'say new and different things'
rubrics_metrics.description: Great art, whether expressing itself in words, colors, or stones, does not say the same thing over and over again; the merit ... consists in its saying new and different things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition and slavish copying of past models is not a mark of genius. Evaluate works for their capacity to offer something new rather than merely repeat established motifs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule- or model-based production is manufacture, not art
rubrics_metrics.description: Exactly so far as architecture works on known rules, and from given models, it is not an art, but a manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a building is produced by rote copying (e.g., lifting capitals or mouldings from canonical examples) it should be judged as craftsmanship rather than creative art; originality and inventive application of principles count higher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change/variety as a necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Change or variety is as much a necessity to the human heart and brain in buildings as in books; there is no merit, though there is some occasional use, in monotony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess architectural schemes for presence of considered variety; an architecture of strict monotony gives neither pleasure nor profit except in limited, deliberate uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Healthy vs diseased love of change
rubrics_metrics.description: We must note the distinction between a healthy and a diseased love of change; the diseased love of change destroyed Gothic where it was abused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Healthy variety arises where it serves purpose or emerges naturally; diseased variety is excessive, frequent, or fantastical. Use analogies (music) to judge whether variations are tempered by structure and patience or are mere caprice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotony's legitimate use — to value change ('transparent monotony')
rubrics_metrics.description: Monotony in certain measure, used in order to give value to change, and, above all, that 'transparent' monotony ... is an essential in architectural as in all other composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monotony should not be judged always negatively; it can provide sublimity and a stage for variation. Evaluate patience demanded of the observer and whether the monotony makes the subsequent change more rewarding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talent is shown in changes, not in monotony
rubrics_metrics.description: The talent of the composer is not in the monotony, but in the changes ... it is always in the new arrangement or invention that his intellect is shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing creative skill, prioritize evidence of invention and imaginative rearrangement over mere endurance of repeated forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gothic as architecture of perpetual novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The Gothic spirit ... invented a series of forms of which the merit was ... _capable of perpetual novelty_. The pointed arch ... admitted of millions of variations ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value architectural types that permit endless, context-sensitive variation (e.g., pointed arch, grouped shafts, tracery) — this adaptability is a virtue, especially in Gothic tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function and practical necessity over enforced symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: They never suffered ideas of outside symmetries and consistencies to interfere with the real use and value of what they did. If they wanted a window, they opened one ... utterly regardless of any established conventionalities of external appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge interventions that prioritize use, surprise, or internal necessity (an 'unexpected' window, added room, buttress) positively even when they break formal symmetry; irregularity for functional or narrative interest is defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalism — frank representation of natural objects
rubrics_metrics.description: NATURALISM; that is to say, the love of natural objects for their own sake, and the effort to represent them frankly, unconstrained by artistical laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate fidelity to observed nature where appropriate — Gothic (Western) tendencies favor factual representation as legitimate material for ornament and form, though not without balancing with design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between abstract composition and representation of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The arrangement of colors and lines is an art analogous to the composition of music, and entirely independent of the representation of facts ... Good coloring does not necessarily convey the image of anything but itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess color/line/ornament both as autonomous composition and as imitation of fact; excellence can exist in pure composition independent of representational accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noblest art unites abstract value with imitative power
rubrics_metrics.description: The noblest art is an exact unison of the abstract value, with the imitative power, of forms and colors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer works that achieve both strong compositional (abstract) qualities and convincing representation of subject-matter; identify whether a work leans toward one pole and whether that is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three artist-types: men of facts / men of design / men of both
rubrics_metrics.description: Men are universally divided ... into three great classes; on the right side are the men of facts, on the left the men of design, in the centre the men of both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this typology to classify work: fact-focused pieces (accurate natural record), design-focused pieces (ornamental/compositional invention), and central works (combine both). Each class has healthy roles and contexts of appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error: men of facts despise design
rubrics_metrics.description: When the men of facts despise design. This is the error of the common Dutch painters ... who suppose that all is done when the imitation is perfected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat purely imitative work that rejects compositional study as limited and potentially dead; historical example: some English landscapists who value faithful atmospheric effect to the exclusion of composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error: men of design despise facts
rubrics_metrics.description: When the men of design despise facts ... the best colorist invents best by taking hints from natural colors; if the truths of nature are wilfully neglected, the intellect becomes comparatively decrepit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warn against decorative invention that abandons contact with natural truth (example: some Chinese ornament in Ruskin's view); evaluate whether decorative choices impoverish the work's vitality by denying factual basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error: men of facts envy design (plagiarism and fungous growth)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the men of facts envy design ... strive to obtain the inventive powers which nature has denied them ... perish in a fungous growth of plagiarism and laws of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify works where imitators attempt composition beyond their powers, producing derivative, plagiaristic art; this was a major error of Ruskin's present century.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error: men of design envy facts (over-imitative ornament)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the men of design envy facts; ... the temptation of closely imitating nature leads them to forget their own proper ornamental function ... as in the hawthorn moulding ... which might have been better if not painted green.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique ornamental design that sacrifices compositional function to slavish natural imitation; ornamental work should not become mere literal copy of nature at expense of its architectural purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative harm: fact-based pathologies injure the public more
rubrics_metrics.description: The two morbid conditions to which the men of the facts are liable are much more dangerous and harmful than those to which the men of design are liable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating cultural impact, consider that fact-only iconoclasm (rejecting design) can cause broader social damage (e.g., 'modern English fact-hunter' vs. merely self-limiting decorative errors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three moral attitudes to facts: Purists / Naturalists / Sensualists
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything presented to them in nature has good and evil mingled in it ... Purists take the good and leave the evil; Naturalists perceive and pursue the good and evil together; Sensualists perceive and imitate evil only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these moral/esthetic categories to judge selection and attitude toward subject-matter: Purists idealize and omit harshness; Naturalists include the full range balancedly; Sensualists revel in evil and degrade art's moral function. Examples: Angelico (Purist), Turner (Naturalist), Caravaggio/Salvator Rosa (Sensualists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of art to function (sometimes facts without art, or art without facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best art is not always wanted. Facts are often wanted without art, as in a geological diagram; and art often without facts, as in a Turkey carpet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a work, consider its intended purpose: did it aim to inform (favor facts) or to decorate/compose (favor design)? Excellence should be judged in light of that purpose rather than by a single universal standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confession of Imperfection and Desire of Change as essential Gothic elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The confession of Imperfection and the confession of Desire of Change ... the work of the Gothic heart is fretwork still, and it can neither rest in, nor from, its labor, but must pass on, sleeplessly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate Gothic works for signs that they express human imperfection and restless striving — buildings that acknowledge incompletion or change (additions, variations across time) embody key Gothic values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gothic flexibility — fitting diverse services without loss of unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic is ... that which can fit itself most easily to all services, vulgar or noble ... it can shrink into a turret, expand into a hall, coil into a staircase, or spring into a spire, with undegraded grace and unexhausted energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value designs that accommodate diverse functional needs while retaining expressive unity and energy; adaptability to changing requirements is a mark of rational, living architecture.
